title: Vectors, Matrices and Linear Systems
description: Vectors and norms, matrices as linear maps, matrix products, Gaussian elimination, inverses, determinants and LU factorization.
overview: Linear algebra is the language of data. A data point is a vector, a data set is a matrix, a linear model is a matrix–vector product, and a layer of a neural network is a matrix multiplication followed by a nonlinearity. Solving least squares, running PCA and analyzing the stability of gradient descent all reduce to questions about matrices.

This chapter covers the mechanics: vectors, norms and angles; matrices and their products from several viewpoints; solving linear systems by elimination; inverses and determinants; and the LU factorization that is used in practice. The next chapters give the structure behind these mechanics: subspaces, orthogonality, eigenvalues and the singular value decomposition.
objectives: Compute dot products, norms, distances and angles of vectors, and state the Cauchy–Schwarz and triangle inequalities.
Multiply matrices, interpret the product as composition of linear maps, and use the column and outer-product views.
Solve a linear system by Gaussian elimination and decide whether it has no, one or infinitely many solutions.
Compute a 2×2 inverse and a determinant, and state what the determinant means geometrically.
Factor a matrix as LU and use it to solve systems.

sections.title: Vectors, dot products and norms
body: A **vector** in ℝⁿ is an ordered list of n real numbers, x = (x₁, …, x_n). It can be viewed as a point, or as an arrow from the origin. Vectors are added and scaled component by component, and a **linear combination** is a sum c₁v₁ + … + c_kv_k. In machine learning a vector holds the features of an example, or the weights of a model.

Here is a concrete use. A house with 120 square meters and 3 bedrooms is the vector (120, 3). A pricing rule that charges 2 per square meter and 10 per bedroom is the vector (2, 10). The price is 120 · 2 + 3 · 10 = 270, the sum of the products of matching entries. That sum is the dot product, and it is large when the features are big where the weights are big, which is why it measures how well two vectors line up.
The **dot product** (inner product) of x and y is

body.eq: x · y = xᵀy = Σ_i x_i y_i = ‖x‖ ‖y‖ cos θ

body: where θ is the angle between them. It is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular (orthogonal). A linear model's prediction wᵀx is a dot product, a measure of how well the input aligns with the weights.
A **norm** ‖x‖ measures length. The standard ones are

eqs: ℓ1 norm, the sum of absolute values; promotes sparsity when penalized

body: Each satisfies ‖x‖ ≥ 0 with equality only for x = 0, ‖cx‖ = |c|‖x‖, and the **triangle inequality** ‖x + y‖ ≤ ‖x‖ + ‖y‖. The distance between x and y is ‖x − y‖. A **unit vector** has norm 1. The **Cauchy–Schwarz inequality** bounds the dot product:
It is what makes cos θ = x·y/(‖x‖‖y‖) lie between −1 and 1, and so makes the angle well defined. The cosine of the angle is the cosine similarity used to compare documents and embeddings.

body.tip: Normalizing a vector to unit length (dividing by its norm) turns the dot product into the cosine similarity, and Euclidean distance between unit vectors into √(2 − 2cos θ): the two comparisons rank pairs in the same order.

sections.title: Matrices and matrix products
body: Think of a matrix as a machine: a vector goes in, another vector comes out. For example, the matrix [[0, −1], [1, 0]] takes the arrow (1, 0) to (0, 1) and (0, 1) to (−1, 0), so it rotates every arrow by 90° counterclockwise. A different matrix might stretch, flip or squash the plane. Multiplying two matrices means running one machine after the other. An m × n **matrix** A is a rectangular array with m rows and n columns. It can be read in two ways: as a table of data (rows are examples, columns are features), or as a **linear map** x ↦ Ax from ℝⁿ to ℝᵐ. The map is linear: A(cx + dy) = cAx + dAy. Every linear map between finite-dimensional spaces is a matrix.
The **product** AB of an m × k matrix and a k × n matrix is the m × n matrix whose entries are dot products of rows of A with columns of B:

The product corresponds to composing the maps: (AB)x = A(Bx). The inner dimensions must match. Matrix multiplication is associative, (AB)C = A(BC), and distributive, but **not commutative**: in general AB ≠ BA.

example.title: A product that does not commute

body.h: Three ways to see a product

list: **Entry view**: each entry is a row-times-column dot product.

**Column view**: Ax is a linear combination of the columns of A, with coefficients from x: Ax = x₁a₁ + … + x_na_n. So the set of possible outputs is the span of the columns. Each column of AB is A times a column of B.

**Outer-product view**: AB = Σ_l (column l of A)(row l of B), a sum of rank-one matrices. The outer product uvᵀ of two vectors is a matrix with entries u_iv_j. This is how the gradient of a weight matrix, δaᵀ, arises in backpropagation.

body: The **transpose** Aᵀ swaps rows and columns: (Aᵀ)_ij = A_ji, with (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ (order reverses). Some special matrices:

list: The **identity matrix** I has ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; AI = IA = A.
A **diagonal matrix** has non-zeros only on the diagonal. Multiplying by diag(d) scales each coordinate. Powers are cheap: diag(d)ᵏ = diag(dᵏ).
A **symmetric** matrix satisfies Aᵀ = A. Covariance matrices, XᵀX and Hessians are symmetric.
An **orthogonal** matrix has QᵀQ = I: its columns are orthonormal, and it preserves lengths and angles (a rotation or reflection).
A **triangular** matrix has zeros above or below the diagonal; systems with triangular matrices are solved easily by substitution.

body: The **trace** tr(A) = Σ A_ii sums the diagonal; it satisfies tr(AB) = tr(BA) and equals the sum of the eigenvalues.

example.title: A layer as a matrix product
example.problem: A batch of m = 100 examples with n = 20 features is stored in X (100 × 20). A layer has 50 units, with weights W (20 × 50). What are the shapes of XW, and how many multiply–adds does it take?
example.solution: XW is 100 × 50. Each of its 5000 entries is a dot product of length 20, so the cost is 100 · 20 · 50 = 100,000 multiply–adds. In general, an (m × k)(k × n) product costs mkn.

sections.title: Linear systems and Gaussian elimination
body: A **linear system** of m equations in n unknowns is Ax = b. The row picture is that each equation is a hyperplane and a solution lies on all of them. The column picture is that we look for coefficients x for which b is a linear combination of the columns of A.

body.caption: Each equation is a line. The system x + y = 3, x − y = 1 has exactly one solution, where the lines cross.

body: **Gaussian elimination** turns Ax = b into an equivalent triangular system by **row operations**: swap two rows, scale a row, or add a multiple of one row to another. These do not change the solutions. Use the first equation to eliminate x₁ from the others, the next to eliminate x₂, and so on. The leading non-zero entry of each row is a **pivot**. The triangular system is then solved by **back substitution**, from the last equation upward.

example.title: Solving a 3 × 3 system
example.problem: Solve x + y + z = 3, 2x + 3y + z = 6, x + 2y + 3z = 6.
solution: Eliminate x: R₂ − 2R₁ gives y − z = 0. R₃ − R₁ gives y + 2z = 3.
Eliminate y: (R₃ − R₁) − (R₂ − 2R₁) gives 3z = 3, so z = 1.
Back substitute: y − 1 = 0 gives y = 1, and x + 1 + 1 = 3 gives x = 1. The solution is (1, 1, 1).

body: A system has no solution when elimination produces an equation 0 = c with c ≠ 0 (the equations are inconsistent), exactly one solution when every unknown has a pivot, and infinitely many when some unknown has no pivot (a **free variable**). Counting pivots gives the **rank**, discussed in the next chapter. Elimination on an n × n system costs about (2/3)n³ operations, so that doubling n multiplies the time by 8.

example.title: No solution and infinitely many solutions
example.problem: Classify x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = 5, and x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = 4.
example.solution: In the first system, subtracting twice the first equation from the second gives 0 = 1: inconsistent, no solution (two parallel lines). In the second, the same step gives 0 = 0: the equations are the same line, y is free, and the solutions are (2 − y, y) for any y.

sections.title: Inverses and determinants
body: A square matrix A is **invertible** if there is a matrix A⁻¹ with A⁻¹A = AA⁻¹ = I. Then Ax = b has the unique solution x = A⁻¹b. A matrix with no inverse is **singular**. Useful rules: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹ and (Aᵀ)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)ᵀ. For a 2 × 2 matrix,

example.title: A 2 × 2 inverse
example.problem: Invert A = [[2, 1], [5, 3]] and use it to solve Ax = (1, 2).

body: Geometrically, the matrix [[2, 0], [0, 3]] stretches the plane by 2 horizontally and 3 vertically, so the unit square becomes a 2 by 3 rectangle: area is multiplied by 6, and the determinant is 6. A matrix like [[1, 2], [2, 4]] squashes the whole plane onto a single line, so area becomes 0, the determinant is 0, and the squashing cannot be undone. The **determinant** det A is a number that tests invertibility and measures volume change. For 2 × 2 it is ad − bc. For larger matrices, it is computed by elimination: det A is the product of the pivots, up to the sign changes caused by row swaps.

list: **A is invertible if and only if det A ≠ 0.**
The linear map x ↦ Ax scales volumes by |det A|, and the sign records whether orientation is reversed. A det of 0 means the map squashes space onto a lower dimension, and information is lost.
det(AB) = det A · det B, det Aᵀ = det A, det(A⁻¹) = 1/det A, and for a triangular matrix det is the product of the diagonal.
det A is the product of the eigenvalues.

example.title: Determinant from pivots
example.problem: Find the determinant of the coefficient matrix [[1, 1, 1], [2, 3, 1], [1, 2, 3]] from the earlier example.
example.solution: The pivots found during elimination are 1, 1 and 3, so det = 1 · 1 · 3 = 3 (no row swaps). The matrix is invertible, as we saw from the unique solution.

body.warn: Avoid computing A⁻¹ explicitly to solve Ax = b. Solving by elimination or an LU factorization is faster and more accurate. The inverse appears in formulas such as (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy, but is implemented as a solve.

sections.title: LU factorization
body: Elimination can be recorded as a factorization. Gaussian elimination reduces A to an upper triangular matrix U, and the multipliers used are stored in a lower triangular matrix L with ones on its diagonal:

example.title: LU of the earlier matrix
solution: In the elimination above the multipliers were 2 (for R₂ − 2R₁), 1 (for R₃ − R₁) and 1 (for R₃ − R₂). They go below the diagonal of L:

body: To solve Ax = b, solve two triangular systems: first Ly = b by **forward substitution**, and then Ux = y by back substitution. Each costs only O(n²). The O((2/3)n³) factorization is done once, so a new right-hand side is cheap, which is useful when the same matrix is used with many b's. In practice rows are swapped for numerical stability (partial pivoting), giving PA = LU with a permutation matrix P.

list: For a symmetric positive definite matrix, such as XᵀX or a covariance matrix, the **Cholesky factorization** A = LLᵀ is twice as fast as LU and numerically stable. It is the standard way to solve the normal equations and to sample from a multivariate Gaussian.
The determinant is the product of the diagonal of U (and the sign of P).
Orthogonal factorizations (QR, SVD) are more stable for least squares and are covered in the next chapters.

quiz.q: What is the cosine of the angle between x = (3, 4) and y = (4, 3)?
quiz.why: x·y = 12 + 12 = 24 and ‖x‖‖y‖ = 5 · 5 = 25, so cos θ = 24/25 = 0.96. The value 24 is the dot product without dividing by the norms.

quiz.q: For x = (−6, 8), what are ‖x‖_∞, ‖x‖₂ and ‖x‖₁ in that order?
quiz.why: The largest absolute entry is 8, √(36 + 64) = 10, and |−6| + |8| = 14. The sum 2 results from forgetting the absolute values in the ℓ1 norm.

quiz.q: Two vectors have ‖x‖₂ = 2 and ‖y‖₂ = 3. Which value of x·y is impossible?
quiz.why: Cauchy–Schwarz gives |x·y| ≤ 2 · 3 = 6. A value of 6 occurs when the vectors are parallel, and 0 when they are perpendicular.

quiz.q: Vectors x and y are orthogonal, with ‖x‖₂ = 3 and ‖y‖₂ = 4. What is ‖x + y‖₂?
quiz.why: ‖x + y‖² = ‖x‖² + 2x·y + ‖y‖² = 9 + 0 + 16 = 25. The triangle inequality only bounds the norm by 7, and equality there needs parallel vectors.

quiz.q: Let A = [[1, 0], [2, 3]] and B = [[4, 1], [0, 2]]. Which matrix is AB?
quiz.why: Row 2 of A is (2, 3), so AB has row 2 = 2·(4, 1) + 3·(0, 2) = (8, 8). The matrix BA is the first wrong option, and the entrywise product is the second.
Ax = 2·(1, 3, 5) − 1·(2, 4, 6) = (0, 2, 4): a combination of the columns with coefficients from x. Swapping the coefficients gives (3, 5, 7).

quiz.q: For u = (1, 2) and v = (3, 4, 5), what is the entry in row 2, column 3 of the outer product uvᵀ?
quiz.why: (uvᵀ)_ij = u_i v_j, so the entry is u₂v₃ = 2 · 5 = 10. The other options are u₂v₂, u₂v₁ and u₁v₃.

quiz.q: Q = [[0.6, −0.8], [0.8, 0.6]] satisfies QᵀQ = I. What is ‖Qx‖₂ for x = (3, 4)?
quiz.why: An orthogonal matrix preserves length, so ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖ = 5. Directly, Qx = (−1.4, 4.8), whose ℓ2 norm is 5. The value 6.2 is its ℓ1 norm.

quiz.q: For which value of k does the system x + 2y = 4, 3x + 6y = k have a solution?
quiz.a: Only k = 12, and then infinitely many
wrong: Every k, with a unique solution
quiz.why: Eliminating gives 0 = k − 12. This is consistent only when k = 12, leaving y free. For any other k the equations contradict each other.

quiz.q: What is the solution (x, y) of x + 2y = 5, 3x + 4y = 11?
quiz.why: R₂ − 3R₁ gives −2y = −4, so y = 2 and x = 1. Each wrong option satisfies the first equation but fails the second.

quiz.q: Dense elimination on a 1000 × 1000 system takes 2 seconds. About how long does a 3000 × 3000 system take?
quiz.why: The cost grows like n³, and tripling n multiplies the time by 3³ = 27, so 2 × 27 = 54 seconds. A factor of 9 would correspond to n².

quiz.q: A consistent system of 3 equations in 5 unknowns reduces to 3 pivots. How many free variables does it have?
quiz.why: Unknowns without a pivot are free: 5 − 3 = 2. With any free variable a consistent system has infinitely many solutions.

quiz.q: Which matrix is the inverse of A = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]?
quiz.why: ad − bc = 4 − 6 = −2, so A⁻¹ = (1/−2)[[4, −2], [−3, 1]]. The last option forgets the factor 1/det, and the first has the wrong overall sign.

quiz.q: A 3 × 3 matrix A has det A = 4. What is det(2A)?
quiz.why: Doubling the matrix doubles each of the 3 rows, and the determinant is multiplied by 2 for each, so 2³ · 4 = 32.

quiz.q: Elimination on a 3 × 3 matrix gives pivots 2, 3 and 4 after one row swap. What is the determinant?
quiz.why: The determinant is the product of the pivots, 2 · 3 · 4 = 24, with a sign change for each row swap, here one swap, so −24.

quiz.q: For which value of k is the matrix [[1, 2], [2, k]] singular?
quiz.why: det = k − 4, which vanishes at k = 4. Then the second row is twice the first, and the map squashes the plane onto a line.

quiz.q: A = LU with L = [[1, 0], [3, 1]] and U = [[1, 2], [0, 2]]. What is the solution of Ax = (3, 10)?
quiz.why: Forward: y = (3, 10 − 9) = (3, 1). Back: x₂ = 0.5 and x₁ = 3 − 2(0.5) = 2. The option (3, 1) is the intermediate y, and (−7, 26) results from solving with U before L.

quiz.q: For which matrix is Cholesky factorization A = LLᵀ the appropriate, faster alternative to LU?
quiz.a: XᵀX, where X has linearly independent columns
quiz.why: Cholesky needs a symmetric positive definite matrix. XᵀX is one when X has independent columns, whereas [[0, 1], [1, 0]] is symmetric but has eigenvalues of both signs.

summary: A vector is a list of numbers. The dot product x·y = ‖x‖‖y‖cos θ; norms ‖·‖₁, ‖·‖₂, ‖·‖_∞; triangle and Cauchy–Schwarz inequalities.

A matrix is a linear map. The product AB composes maps, costs mkn, is associative but not commutative, and (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ. View it by entries, by columns (linear combinations) or as a sum of outer products.
Gaussian elimination solves Ax = b with row operations and back substitution, at cost about (2/3)n³. Solutions may be none, one or infinitely many.
A is invertible iff det A ≠ 0; |det A| is the volume scale factor. Do not form inverses explicitly; solve.
A = LU stores elimination so that new right-hand sides cost O(n²). Cholesky A = LLᵀ is used for symmetric positive definite matrices.

problems.q: Solve 2x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 by elimination.
problems.solution: Add the equations: 3x = 6, so x = 2. Then y = x − 1 = 1.

problems.q: Show that the matrix [[1, 2], [2, 4]] is singular and describe the solutions of [[1, 2], [2, 4]]x = (3, 6).
problems.solution: det = 4 − 4 = 0. The second equation is twice the first, so there is one independent equation x + 2y = 3 with infinitely many solutions (3 − 2y, y).
problems.a: Singular (det 0); infinitely many solutions on the line x + 2y = 3.

problems.q: A and B are 2 × 2 with det A = 3 and det B = −2. Find det(AB), det(A⁻¹) and det(2A).
problems.solution: det(AB) = 3(−2) = −6. det(A⁻¹) = 1/3. For a 2 × 2 matrix, scaling by 2 multiplies each of the two rows by 2, so det(2A) = 2² · 3 = 12.
Forward: Ly = b gives y₁ = 1 and 2y₁ + y₂ = 4, so y₂ = 2. Back: Ux = y gives −2x₂ = 2, so x₂ = −1, and x₁ + 3(−1) = 1, so x₁ = 4.
